Petrushkin, 142 F.4th 1241 (9th Cir. 2025). A current client, Marcus Rennick, is serving a sentence in the Eastern District of Washington under an identical legal theory: the district court applied the U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1(c)(1) cross-reference enhancement based on a finding that Rennick's possessed firearm 'potentially emboldened or facilitated' a separate drug trafficking offense. Rennick's plea agreement contains an appeal waiver nearly identical to Petrushkin's, permitting appeal 'only the reasonableness of his sentence.' Rennick timely filed a notice of appeal, and the Ninth Circuit has requested a briefing schedule on the threshold question of whether the appeal waiver bars the challenge to the § 2K2.1(c)(1) enhancement. The partner needs a comprehensive legal memorandum analyzing whether the Petrushkin panel's holding on appeal waiver scope controls Rennick's case, and if so, how the 'potentially emboldened or facilitated' standard applies on remand. Draft the memorandum to the partner. Do not invent any facts, case citations, party names, or legal standards beyond what appears in the attached opinion. Structure the memo with standard headings: Question Presented, Short Answer, Background, Discussion, and Conclusion. The discussion must address both the appeal-waiver issue and the substantive enhancement standard. The memorandum should be 1,200–1,800 words.

paragraphs: Vincent Nicholas Petrushkin pled guilty to possession of a firearm as a felon in violation of 18 U.S.C. §§ 922(g)(1) and 924(a)(2). The case originated in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Washington, with District Judge Thomas O. Rice presiding. Petrushkin appealed his sentence to the Ninth Circuit.

At sentencing, the district court applied an enhancement pursuant to U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1(c)(1), a cross-reference provision. That provision allows courts to apply the base offense level and special offense characteristics from another substantive offense where the defendant 'used or possessed any firearm or ammunition cited in the offense of conviction in connection with the commission or attempted commission of another offense, or possessed or transferred a firearm or ammunition cited in the offense of conviction with knowledge or intent that it would be used or possessed in connection with another offense.'

The case was argued and submitted on September 11, 2024, in Seattle, Washington. The panel consisted of Circuit Judges William A. Fletcher and Jennifer Sung, and District Judge Jed S. Rakoff of the Southern District of New York, sitting by designation. Judge Sung authored the opinion, which was filed on July 14, 2025.

Petrushkin's plea agreement contained an appeal waiver permitting him to 'appeal only the reasonableness of his sentence.' On appeal, Petrushkin challenged the district court's application of the § 2K2.1(c)(1) enhancement.

paragraphs:
A. Appeal Waiver Does Not Bar the § 2K2.1(c)(1) Enhancement Challenge

The threshold question is whether the appeal waiver in Rennick's plea agreement bars his challenge to the § 2K2.1(c)(1) enhancement. The waiver in Petrushkin's agreement permitted him to 'appeal only the reasonableness of his sentence.' The Ninth Circuit panel held that this language did not waive Petrushkin's right to appeal the district court's application of the (c)(1) enhancement. The rationale is that a challenge to the legal correctness of a sentencing enhancement is distinct from a challenge to the overall reasonableness of the sentence imposed. Because the waiver was limited to reasonableness, it did not encompass a challenge to the district court's legal interpretation and application of the Guidelines.

Because Rennick's plea agreement contains a substantively identical waiver—permitting appeal 'only the reasonableness of his sentence'—Petrushkin's holding directly controls. The appeal waiver does not bar Rennick's challenge to the § 2K2.1(c)(1) enhancement. The appeal may proceed to the merits.

B. The 'Potentially Emboldened or Facilitated' Standard

Having established jurisdiction, the substantive standard governing the § 2K2.1(c)(1) enhancement is the 'potentially emboldened or facilitated' requirement set forth in United States v. Routon, 25 F.3d 815 (9th Cir. 1994). Under Routon, the government must demonstrate that the firearm possessed in connection with the offense of conviction 'potentially emboldened or facilitated' the commission of the separate offense. This standard requires more than mere proximity of the firearm to criminal activity; there must be a functional nexus between the firearm and the other offense.

The Petrushkin panel applied the Routon standard and concluded that the district court had erred in its application of the § 2K2.1(c)(1) enhancement. The panel vacated Petrushkin's sentence and remanded the case for resentencing. On remand, the district court will be required to apply the Routon 'potentially emboldened or facilitated' standard to determine whether the enhancement is warranted.

For Rennick's case, the same standard governs. On remand, the district court must find that Rennick's firearm 'potentially emboldened or facilitated' the separate drug trafficking offense before applying the § 2K2.1(c)(1) cross-reference enhancement. The government bears the burden of establishing this nexus by a preponderance of the evidence.
